learning_goal: State the attachments, nerve supply and actions of rectus abdominis, point to its two borders and say what happens at each, and explain why a midline incision, a paramedian incision and a Pfannenstiel incision have completely different consequences for the muscle and its nerves.

terms: anterior wall of the rectus sheath
posterior wall of the rectus sheath

structures.name: right rectus abdominis
structures.label: Rectus abdominis (right)
structures.narration: A long strap running the whole height of the front of the abdomen, from the pubis to the costal margin. Note its shape: broad and thin at the top, narrow and thick at the bottom. It arises from the pubic crest and the front of the pubic symphysis, and inserts into the fifth, sixth and seventh costal cartilages and the xiphoid process. It is the only vertical muscle of the abdominal wall — everything else runs obliquely or across.

structures.name: left rectus abdominis
structures.label: Rectus abdominis (left)
structures.narration: The mirror image, separated from its partner only by the linea alba. The two recti are never joined: they lie side by side in their own sheaths, which is why a midline incision passes between them without cutting either one.

structures.name: linea alba
structures.label: Linea alba
structures.narration: The white line down the middle, where the aponeuroses of the three flat muscles from both sides interlace. It is almost bloodless, which is why the midline is the fastest way into the abdomen in an emergency. It is broad above the umbilicus and narrow below it. Small gaps in it let extraperitoneal fat through as an epigastric hernia, and when it stretches in pregnancy or obesity the two recti drift apart — divarication, which bulges on sitting up but is not a true hernia and does not strangulate.

structures.name: right pyramidalis
structures.label: Pyramidalis (right)
terms: in front of the lower rectus
structures.narration: A small triangle in front of the lowest part of the rectus, inside the same sheath, running from the pubic crest up into the linea alba. It tenses the linea alba and does very little else. It is absent in about a fifth of people, and it is the surgeon's marker for the midline at the bottom of the wound.

structures.name: left pyramidalis
structures.label: Pyramidalis (left)
terms: may be absent on one side
structures.narration: The same on the left, and it may be present on one side and missing on the other. Nothing depends on it clinically except that it tells you where the midline is.

structures.label: Origin — pubic crest
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: nearest CONTACT point between the right rectus abdominis and the right hip bone — the origin from the pubic crest and the front of the pubic symphysis (gap 0.29 mm); see tools/derive-abdominal-wall-landmarks.mjs
structures.narration: The muscle starts here by a short tendon from the pubic crest and the front of the symphysis. It is at its narrowest and thickest at this point. A Pfannenstiel incision crosses just above this, which is why the recti can be pulled apart in the midline rather than cut.

structures.label: Insertion — fifth costal cartilage
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: nearest CONTACT point between the right rectus abdominis and the right fifth costal cartilage — the highest of its three costal insertions (gap 0.35 mm); see tools/derive-abdominal-wall-landmarks.mjs
structures.narration: The highest and most lateral of the three costal attachments. Follow the muscle up and it spreads out to grip the fifth, sixth and seventh cartilages in that order, moving medially as it goes. This is why the upper abdomen is where a rectus is broad and a hernia through the linea alba is small.

structures.label: Insertion — sixth costal cartilage
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: nearest CONTACT point between the right rectus abdominis and the right sixth costal cartilage — the middle of its three costal insertions (gap 0.17 mm); see tools/derive-abdominal-wall-landmarks.mjs
structures.narration: The middle attachment, sitting medial to the fifth. The seventh cartilage and the xiphoid take the most medial fibres and complete the fan.

structures.label: Upper end — broad and thin
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: the highest (most superior) vertex of the right rectus abdominis, 181.9 mm from its surface centroid — the top of the muscle, where it is broad and thin against the costal margin; see tools/derive-abdominal-wall-landmarks.mjs
structures.narration: Up here the muscle is wide and flat. Remember the taper — broad and thin above, narrow and thick below — and you can predict where a rectus sheath haematoma will be tense and painful and where it will simply spread.

structures.label: Lower end — narrow and thick
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: the lowest (most inferior) vertex of the right rectus abdominis, 220.2 mm from its surface centroid — the bottom of the muscle at the pubis, where it is narrow and thick; see tools/derive-abdominal-wall-landmarks.mjs
structures.narration: Down here the muscle is narrow and thick, and it is packed into the tightest part of the sheath. The inferior epigastric artery enters the sheath just above the pubis and runs up behind the muscle. A sudden cough tearing that vessel gives the classic rectus sheath haematoma: a painful lump that does not move when the patient tenses, and does not cross the midline.

structures.label: Linea semilunaris — the lateral border
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: the most lateral (most body-right) vertex of the right rectus abdominis, 94.5 mm from its surface centroid — the lateral border, which is the linea semilunaris; see tools/derive-abdominal-wall-landmarks.mjs
structures.narration: The curved lateral edge of the muscle, visible on a lean abdomen. Three things happen along it. The aponeuroses of the flat muscles split here to form the sheath. The nerves and vessels enter the sheath here, so a wide lateral dissection denervates the muscle. And a Spigelian hernia comes through here, just below the level of the umbilicus, hiding under an intact external oblique — which is why it is felt as a vague lump and missed.

structures.label: Closest approach to the midline
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: the single most medial (most body-left) vertex of the right rectus abdominis, 189.4 mm from its surface centroid. The medial border is a line, not a point, and its most medial point is at the PUBIC end where the two recti converge — which is where this lands, and why the label reads "closest approach to the midline" rather than "the linea alba"; see tools/derive-abdominal-wall-landmarks.mjs
terms: the recti converge at the pubis
structures.narration: The two recti are furthest apart in the epigastrium and closest together at the pubis — this is the point where they nearly meet. That is why the linea alba is broad above and narrow below, and why divarication of the recti shows in the upper abdomen and epigastric hernias occur there and not down here.

structures.label: Anterior wall of the rectus sheath
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: nearest CONTACT point between the right rectus abdominis and the right external oblique — where the external oblique aponeurosis lies against the muscle as the anterior wall of the rectus sheath (gap 0.34 mm); see tools/derive-abdominal-wall-landmarks.mjs
structures.narration: The external oblique aponeurosis passes in front of the muscle here and never behind it — at every level, the anterior wall of the sheath contains external oblique. The tendinous intersections are stuck to this front wall and free from the back, which is why the six-pack shows through the skin and why blood in the sheath is trapped in compartments above the umbilicus but free to track below it.

structures.name: right external oblique
structures.label: External oblique (right)
structures.narration: The outermost flat muscle, its fibres running downwards and forwards — hands-in-pockets direction. Its aponeurosis is always in front of the rectus. Its lower free border rolls back on itself to become the inguinal ligament.

structures.name: left external oblique
structures.label: External oblique (left)
structures.narration: Its aponeurosis meets the one from the other side in the linea alba and the fibres interlace across the midline. That interlacing is what holds the two halves of the wall together.

structures.name: right internal oblique
structures.label: Internal oblique — right
terms: fibres at right angles to external oblique
structures.narration: The middle layer, its fibres running at right angles to the external oblique. Its aponeurosis is the one that splits: above the arcuate line it goes both in front of and behind the rectus, below the line it goes entirely in front. That single behaviour is the whole rectus sheath.

structures.name: right transversus abdominis
structures.label: Transversus abdominis — right
structures.narration: The deepest layer, fibres running horizontally, and the one that squeezes the abdomen like a belt. Its aponeurosis is behind the rectus above the arcuate line and in front of it below. The nerves to the wall run between this muscle and the internal oblique, which is the plane a TAP block fills.

structures.name: right fifth costal cartilage
structures.label: Fifth costal cartilage
structures.narration: The highest bar the rectus grips.

structures.name: right sixth costal cartilage
structures.label: Sixth costal cartilage
structures.narration: The middle bar.

structures.name: right seventh costal cartilage
structures.label: Seventh costal cartilage
structures.narration: The lowest and most medial bar, sitting beside the xiphoid at the apex of the subcostal angle.

structures.name: xiphoid process
structures.label: Xiphoid process
terms: upper end of the linea alba
structures.narration: The top of the midline. The linea alba runs from here to the pubic symphysis, and the medial fibres of both recti take hold of it.

structures.name: right hip bone
structures.label: Hip bone (right)
structures.narration: The bottom frame of the wall. The rectus takes origin from the pubic crest and the front of the symphysis; the flat muscles run down to the iliac crest and the inguinal ligament.

structures.name: left hip bone
structures.label: Hip bone (left)
structures.narration: The mirror half. The two pubic crests and the symphysis between them make one continuous origin for both recti.

structures.name: right inguinal ligament
structures.label: Inguinal ligament — right
terms: rolled lower border of external oblique
lower limit of the abdominal wall
structures.narration: The rolled-under lower border of the external oblique aponeurosis, from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle. It marks where the abdominal wall stops and the thigh begins, and it is the floor of the inguinal canal.

structures.name: body of sternum
structures.label: Body of the sternum
structures.narration: For orientation only — the abdominal wall begins where this ends.

views.title: One vertical muscle in a wall of oblique ones
views.narration: The anterior abdominal wall is three flat muscles wrapping round from the sides and one strap running straight up and down in front. That strap is rectus abdominis. Everything difficult about this region — the sheath, the arcuate line, the hernias, the incisions — comes from how the three flat aponeuroses arrange themselves around this one vertical muscle.

views.title: Pubis to costal margin
views.narration: Follow it from the bottom up. It arises from the pubic crest and the front of the pubic symphysis, narrow and thick. It widens as it climbs. It ends by gripping the fifth, sixth and seventh costal cartilages and the xiphoid process, broad and thin. Two sentences, and you have the attachments an examiner will ask for.

views.title: Two borders, two hernias
views.narration: The medial border faces the linea alba; the lateral border is the linea semilunaris. Each has its own hernia. Through the linea alba, above the umbilicus where it is broad, comes the epigastric hernia — a small painful knuckle of fat. Along the linea semilunaris, just below the umbilicus, comes the Spigelian hernia — which burrows under an intact external oblique, so there is nothing to see and only a vague deep fullness to feel. Look at the two recti together and you can also see why they drift apart in pregnancy: nothing joins them except that white line.

views.title: The sheath around it

ops.kind: aponeurosis passes behind, then in front

views.narration: The muscle does not lie loose. The three flat aponeuroses wrap it in a sheath, and the rule has three lines. External oblique is always in front. Transversus is behind above the arcuate line and in front below it. Internal oblique splits and goes both ways above the line, and passes entirely in front below it. So above the arcuate line the sheath has a front and a back; below it, everything is in front and the muscle rests directly on the transversalis fascia and peritoneum.

views.title: What it does when it shortens

ops.kind: pulls the ribs towards the pubis

views.narration: It has two jobs. First, it flexes the trunk: it pulls the ribs down towards the pubis, which is the sit-up. Second, with the flat muscles, it raises intra-abdominal pressure for coughing, vomiting, defaecation and childbirth. Watch the direction of pull in this side view — straight down the front of the body, well in front of the vertebral column, so it has a long lever arm and is a powerful flexor for its size.

views.title: Segmental nerves, and the sign that uses them
views.narration: The muscle is supplied segmentally by the lower six thoracic nerves, T7 to T12. They run between internal oblique and transversus, then pierce the sheath at the lateral border and enter the muscle from behind. Two consequences. A wide lateral incision cuts nerve after nerve and leaves a paralysed bulging wall, so surgeons split muscle rather than cut across it. And because the muscle lies in front of everything inside, tensing it tells you which side of the wall the trouble is on: ask the patient to lift their head off the bed and press again. Tenderness that persists or worsens is arising in the wall itself, which the contraction has brought closer to your hand. Tenderness that eases is inside the abdomen, now shielded by a board of contracted muscle. That is Carnett's sign, and it is a test of position, not of innervation.

views.title: Where a surgeon cuts, and why

ops.kind: marks the midline at the pubis

views.narration: Three incisions, three different relationships to this muscle. The midline incision goes through the linea alba between the two recti: bloodless, fast, no muscle cut, no nerve cut — the emergency laparotomy. The Pfannenstiel goes across the skin just above the pubis, opens the anterior sheath transversely and then separates the recti in the midline, so again nothing is cut across — that is the caesarean section. The old paramedian incision went through the muscle and cost nerves, which is why it has largely been abandoned. Peel the muscles away and what is left is the frame they all hang on.

gaps: The tendinous intersections have no mesh and never will — they are markings on the muscle, not objects. Three of them are usually described, at the xiphoid, the umbilicus and midway between, and they are the reason the six-pack is visible and the reason a rectus sheath haematoma above the umbilicus is compartmentalised while one below it is free to spread. All of that is narration in this scene. A provider that shipped rectus abdominis as several bellies rather than one would let this be shown.

The arcuate line has no mesh either, for the same reason: it is the lower edge of the posterior sheath, a line on a fascia. Beat 4 states the rule above and below it and the cross-section shows the level, but the line itself cannot be drawn. It belongs to the curriculum's separate 'Rectus sheath' entry and is deliberately not claimed as covered here.

There is no rectus sheath in the catalog as an object — only the muscles whose aponeuroses form it. The sheath is therefore taught through relationships between the flat muscles and the rectus, plus one measured anchor where the external oblique actually contacts the muscle. The curriculum's 'Rectus sheath' entry still needs its own scene and this one does not claim it.

The umbilicus is absent from the catalog. It is the reference point for almost every statement about this wall — the arcuate line is midway between it and the pubis, the Spigelian hernia is just below it, divarication shows above it, and it is the T10 dermatome. Every one of those is narrated against attachments that do exist rather than against the umbilicus itself.

No nerve or vessel of the abdominal wall exists in the catalog: not the thoracoabdominal nerves, not the superior or inferior epigastric arteries. Beat 6 traces the segmental nerves as a declared concept along the structures they pass. This is a real teaching loss, because the inferior epigastric artery is both the cause of a rectus sheath haematoma and the landmark that separates a direct from an indirect inguinal hernia.

Only the right side of the wall could be measured. The left rectus, the linea alba, the pyramidales, the xiphoid, the seventh costal cartilage, the internal oblique, the transversus and the inguinal ligament are all in the catalog and are all referenced by this scene, but none of them was on disk when the landmarks were derived, so no landmark was derived from them. As of the 2026-08-28 audit all seventeen models this scene references are on disk, so left-sided and midline landmarks could now be measured rather than left out. Every anchor here is on the right rectus abdominis and says so. Nothing was mirrored across the midline to fake a left-sided landmark.

The 'medial_border' anchor is the single most medial vertex of the muscle, which falls at the pubic end where the two recti converge, not halfway up where a student pictures the medial border. The label and the calibrated_by note both say so rather than rounding the discrepancy away. A true medial border would need an edge-extraction step this tool does not have.
All eight anchors are measured contacts or extremes and every one records how it was placed. All eight remain status 'needs-review' until a human clears them in-app.
